The Government Says You Don't Have a Hiring Problem. Your Practice Says Otherwise.

Jobs and Skills Australia recently released the 2026 Job Shortage List, and to the shock of many in the industry, financial advisers and paraplanners were nowhere to be found. But if you have tried to recruit a qualified paraplanner or a senior administrator in the last twelve months, you know that the official data doesn't match the reality on the ground.

The Financial Advice Association Australia (FAAA) has rightly called for a reconsideration, pointing to "substantial evidence" of a structural skills shortage that has plagued the profession since 2019. While the government relies on "advertised vacancies," small business owners know that the talent pool isn't just shallow; it’s drying up.

The challenge isn't finding candidates.

It's finding qualified professionals with the experience and capacity to support growing financial advice practices.

The 48% Decline and the Five-Year Waiting Room

The numbers tell a stark story. Since 2018, the number of registered advisers in Australia has plummeted from approximately 28,900 to just 15,135 as of March 2026, a massive 48% reduction in less than eight years.

This isn't a temporary dip; it is a structural crisis. Because it now takes a minimum of 4 to 5 years for a new entrant to complete their degree, professional year, and industry exams, there is a "long training gap" that cannot be fixed by local hiring surges in the short term.

Meanwhile, the demand for your time has never been higher. The average adviser now manages 101 recurring clients per year, up from 97 just twelve months ago. This pressure is making the traditional "in-house only" staffing model officially economically unsustainable.

  • Focus on high-value relationships: With the "experience premium" at an all-time high, your time is best spent on client-facing strategy, not back-office processing.

With 3.6 million Australians set to enter retirement over the next decade, the demand for professional guidance is about to explode. There is already an advice gap of 3.1 million Australians over 55 who "need" complex advice but cannot find a provider with the capacity to take them on.
